claim: Clytia hemisphaerica jellyfish have four gonads that lie on the radial canals connecting the manubrium to the circular canal running around the bell rim, adjacent to the tentacle bulbs.
source: (A) Schematic of a Clytia hemisphaerica female jellyfish: The four gonads (g) lie on the radial canals (rc) that connect the manubrium (M) to the circular canal (cc) running around the bell rim, adjacent to the tentacle bulbs (tb).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the figure caption and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Wavelengths between 430 and 520 nm provoked spawning in at least 50% of Clytia gonads.
source: We found that wavelengths between 430 and 520 nm provoked spawning in at least 50% of gonads, with 470–490 nm wavelengths inducing spawning of ≥75% of gonads (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from monochromatic light exposure experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 470–490 nm wavelengths induced spawning of ≥75% of Clytia gonads.
source: We found that wavelengths between 430 and 520 nm provoked spawning in at least 50% of gonads, with 470–490 nm wavelengths inducing spawning of ≥75% of gonads (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from monochromatic light exposure experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Oocyte maturation and subsequent spawning of Clytia female gonads is preferentially triggered by blue-cyan light.
source: Oocyte maturation and subsequent spawning of Clytia female gonads is thus preferentially triggered by blue-cyan light (Figure 1B), the wavelength range which penetrates seawater the deepest (Gehring and Rosbash, 2003; Gühmann et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and cited references.

claim: Blue-cyan light is the wavelength range which penetrates seawater the deepest.
source: Oocyte maturation and subsequent spawning of Clytia female gonads is thus preferentially triggered by blue-cyan light (Figure 1B), the wavelength range which penetrates seawater the deepest (Gehring and Rosbash, 2003; Gühmann et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A total of ten Clytia opsin sequences were identified in transcriptome and genome assemblies.
source: We identified a total of ten Clytia opsin sequences in transcriptome and genome assemblies from Clytia by reciprocal BLAST searches using known hydrozoan opsin sequences (Suga et al., 2008) and by the presence of the diagnostic lysine in the seventh transmembrane domain to which the retinal chromophore binds (Terakita et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis described in the methods.

claim: Opsin9 mRNA was very highly expressed in the gonad ectoderm sample.
source: In the gonad ectoderm sample, two opsin mRNAs (Opsin4 and Opsin7) were detected at low levels and one was very highly expressed (Opsin9), while in the three other gonad samples analysed opsin expression was virtually undetectable (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Opsin4 and Opsin7 mRNAs were detected at low levels in the gonad ectoderm sample.
source: In the gonad ectoderm sample, two opsin mRNAs (Opsin4 and Opsin7) were detected at low levels and one was very highly expressed (Opsin9), while in the three other gonad samples analysed opsin expression was virtually undetectable (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the gonad endoderm, growing oocytes, and fully grown oocytes samples, opsin expression was virtually undetectable.
source: In the gonad ectoderm sample, two opsin mRNAs (Opsin4 and Opsin7) were detected at low levels and one was very highly expressed (Opsin9), while in the three other gonad samples analysed opsin expression was virtually undetectable (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Opsin9 expression was detected in a scattered population of gonad-ectoderm cells.
source: In situ hybridisation of Clytia ovaries revealed Opsin9 expression in a scattered population of gonad-ectoderm cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No Opsin9 expression was detected anywhere else in the medusa besides the gonad ectoderm.
source: No Opsin9 expression was detected anywhere else in the medusa.
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization observations.

claim: Opsin4 and Opsin7 expression could not be detected by in situ hybridisation in Clytia gonads.
source: We were unable to detect by in situ hybridisation in Clytia gonads either of the two lowly-expressed gonad-ectoderm opsin genes, Opsin4 and Opsin7 (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 2D-E.

claim: PP1 and PP4 are two MIH neuropeptide precursor genes co-expressed in a common gonad ectoderm cell population.
source: The distribution of Opsin9-expressing cells was highly reminiscent of the expression pattern for PP1 and PP4 (Figure 2C), the two MIH neuropeptide precursor genes co-expressed in a common gonad ectoderm cell population (Takeda et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takeda et al., 2018 and in situ hybridization data.

claim: 99% of Opsin9 mRNA positive cells were also positive for PP4 mRNA.
source: Double fluorescent in situ hybridisation using probes for Opsin9 and for PP4 revealed that these genes were expressed in the same cells (Figure 2F); 99% of Opsin9 mRNA positive cells were also positive for PP4 mRNA, and over 87% of PP4 mRNA-positive cells were also positive for Opsin9 mRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by double fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Over 87% of PP4 mRNA-positive cells were also positive for Opsin9 mRNA.
source: Double fluorescent in situ hybridisation using probes for Opsin9 and for PP4 revealed that these genes were expressed in the same cells (Figure 2F); 99% of Opsin9 mRNA positive cells were also positive for PP4 mRNA, and over 87% of PP4 mRNA-positive cells were also positive for Opsin9 mRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by double fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Over 86% of cells expressing either Opsin9 or PP4 co-expressed both genes.
source: Of n = 594 randomly chosen cells expressing either gene counted in 10 different gonads, over 86% co-expressed Opsin9 and PP4 mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of double fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The Opsin9n1_4 polyp colony carried a predominant 5 bp deletion corresponding to a frame-shift and premature STOP codon.
source: One of the polyp colonies generated carried a predominant 5 bp deletion, corresponding to a frame-shift and premature STOP codon (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Polyp colony development in the Opsin9n1_4 individual showed no abnormal features.
source: Polyp colony development in this individual, designated Opsin9n1_4 (see Materials and methods), showed no abnormal features.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data during polyp colony development.

claim: Opsin9n1_4 mature medusae did not spawn after the daily dark-light transition.
source: Although these Opsin9n1_4 mature medusae initially appeared normal, they did not spawn after the daily dark-light transition, and after a few days displayed grossly inflated ovaries due to an accumulation of unreleased large immature oocytes with intact GVs (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data and images shown in Figures 3B-C.

claim: Opsin9n1_4 medusae displayed grossly inflated ovaries due to an accumulation of unreleased large immature oocytes with intact GVs.
source: Although these Opsin9n1_4 mature medusae initially appeared normal, they did not spawn after the daily dark-light transition, and after a few days displayed grossly inflated ovaries due to an accumulation of unreleased large immature oocytes with intact GVs (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data and images shown in Figures 3B-C.

claim: Over 85% of Opsin9n1_4 gonads failed to undergo oocyte maturation and spawning upon light stimulation.
source: In three independent experiments to test the light response of isolated gonads, over 85% of Opsin9n1_4 gonads failed to undergo oocyte maturation and spawning upon light stimulation (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Opsin9n1_4 gonads released oocytes in response to synthetic MIH peptide.
source: Opsin9n1_4 gonads did, however, release oocytes in response to synthetic MIH peptide (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Oocytes from Opsin9n1_4 gonads treated with synthetic MIH resumed meiosis normally and could be fertilised.
source: These oocytes resumed meiosis normally and could be fertilised, although the fertilisation rate was lower than for oocytes spawned in parallel from wild type gonads, possibly a consequence of their prolonged retention in the gonad.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of oocyte behavior after MIH treatment.

claim: The fertilisation rate of oocytes from Opsin9n1_4 gonads was lower than for oocytes spawned from wild type gonads.
source: These oocytes resumed meiosis normally and could be fertilised, although the fertilisation rate was lower than for oocytes spawned in parallel from wild type gonads, possibly a consequence of their prolonged retention in the gonad.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing fertilization rates.

claim: The lower fertilisation rate in Opsin9n1_4 oocytes is possibly a consequence of their prolonged retention in the gonad.
source: These oocytes resumed meiosis normally and could be fertilised, although the fertilisation rate was lower than for oocytes spawned in parallel from wild type gonads, possibly a consequence of their prolonged retention in the gonad.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the cause of lower fertilization rates.

claim: Rare gonads from Opsin9n1_4 medusae that spawned after light had greater mosaicism of mutations, with a higher ratio of residual non-frameshift mutations and a significant amount of wild type cells.
source: Genotyping of individual gonads showed that the rare gonads from Opsin9n1_4 medusae that spawned after light had greater mosaicism of mutations, with a higher ratio of residual non-frameshift mutations and also a significant amount of wild type cells, whereas gonads that failed to spawn carried mainly the predominant 5 bp deletion, a second 21 bp deletion and no detectable wild type cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gonads that failed to spawn carried mainly the predominant 5 bp deletion, a second 21 bp deletion and no detectable wild type cells.
source: Genotyping of individual gonads showed that the rare gonads from Opsin9n1_4 medusae that spawned after light had greater mosaicism of mutations, with a higher ratio of residual non-frameshift mutations and also a significant amount of wild type cells, whereas gonads that failed to spawn carried mainly the predominant 5 bp deletion, a second 21 bp deletion and no detectable wild type cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gonad photopigment Opsin9 plays an essential role in light-induced oocyte maturation.
source: The failure of spawning observed in Clytia Opsin9n1_4 mutant jellyfish gonads, together with the absence of detectable Opsin9 expression in non-gonad tissues of the medusa and the autonomous response of isolated wild-type gonads to light, strongly indicates that the gonad photopigment Opsin9 plays an essential role in light-induced oocyte maturation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence including knockout phenotype, expression pattern, and functional assays.

claim: Wild type gonads exhibited a significant decrease of MIH fluorescence values in MIH-Opsin9 cells upon light stimulation.
source: Whereas wild type gonads exhibited a significant decrease of MIH fluorescence values in MIH-Opsin9 cells upon light stimulation (Figure 4A–C), Opsin9 mutant gonads maintained similar levels of MIH fluorescence in both conditions (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: Opsin9 mutant gonads maintained similar levels of MIH fluorescence in both light-adapted and dark-adapted conditions.
source: Whereas wild type gonads exhibited a significant decrease of MIH fluorescence values in MIH-Opsin9 cells upon light stimulation (Figure 4A–C), Opsin9 mutant gonads maintained similar levels of MIH fluorescence in both conditions (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4D-F.

claim: Average MIH fluorescence levels per cell were significantly higher in Opsin9 mutant than in wild type ovaries.
source: Moreover, average MIH fluorescence levels per cell were significantly higher (U test at p<0.01) in Opsin9 mutant than in wild type ovaries suggesting a progressive accumulation of MIH in Opsin9 mutant gonads.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data.

claim: The higher MIH fluorescence levels in Opsin9 mutant ovaries suggest a progressive accumulation of MIH.
source: Moreover, average MIH fluorescence levels per cell were significantly higher (U test at p<0.01) in Opsin9 mutant than in wild type ovaries suggesting a progressive accumulation of MIH in Opsin9 mutant gonads.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the observed higher MIH fluorescence levels.

claim: Opsin9 mutant medusae failed to undergo oocyte maturation and spawning because of reduced MIH secretion in response to light.
source: These immunofluorescence results indicated that Opsin9 mutant medusae failed to undergo oocyte maturation and spawning because of reduced MIH secretion in response to light.
evidence: The claim is inferred from immunofluorescence data showing retained MIH in mutant cells.

claim: Synthetic MIH peptides can reverse the phenotype of Opsin9 mutant gonads.
source: The ability of synthetic MIH peptides to reverse the phenotype of Opsin9 mutant gonads supports this conclusion: Equivalent MIH concentrations to those effective for light-adapted isolated gonads (Takeda et al., 2018) reliably induced oocyte maturation and spawning in Opsin9 mutant isolated gonads (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and cited reference.

claim: The primary defect in Opsin9 mutants is in MIH secretion from the ectoderm following light stimulation.
source: The primary defect in these Opsin9 mutants is thus in MIH secretion from the ectoderm following light stimulation, providing strong evidence that the CRISPR-Cas9 approach had specifically targeted the Opsin9 gene.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of knockout phenotype and rescue experiments.

claim: Opsin9 is required for the MIH-producing cells in the Clytia gonad to release the MIH neuropeptides following dark-light transitions.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Opsin9 is required for the MIH-producing cells in the Clytia gonad to release the MIH neuropeptides following dark-light transitions, and thus has an essential role in light-dependent reproductive control.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including knockout, expression, and functional data.

claim: Opsin9 has an essential role in light-dependent reproductive control.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Opsin9 is required for the MIH-producing cells in the Clytia gonad to release the MIH neuropeptides following dark-light transitions, and thus has an essential role in light-dependent reproductive control.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: The Clytia gonad ectoderm consists of a monolayer of ciliated epitheliomuscular cells.
source: The Clytia gonad ectoderm consists of a monolayer of ciliated epitheliomuscular cells (Leclère and Röttinger, 2017), tightly joined by apical junctions and bearing basal extensions containing muscle fibres.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Epitheliomuscular cells in the gonad ectoderm are tightly joined by apical junctions and bear basal extensions containing muscle fibres.
source: The Clytia gonad ectoderm consists of a monolayer of ciliated epitheliomuscular cells (Leclère and Röttinger, 2017), tightly joined by apical junctions and bearing basal extensions containing muscle fibres.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The cell bodies of the MIH-secreting cells are positioned within the epithelial layer, scattered between the epitheliomuscular cells.
source: The cell bodies of the MIH-secreting cells were found to be positioned within this epithelial layer, scattered between the much more abundant epitheliomuscular cells (Takeda et al., 2018; Figure 5A,B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A, B, D and cited reference.

claim: A variable number of neural-type processes containing prominent microtubule bundles project basally from MIH-secreting cells.
source: A variable number of neural-type processes containing prominent microtubule bundles project basally from these cells (Figure 5E,F), and intermingle with the muscle fibres of surrounding epitheliomuscular cells (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A-C, E-F.

claim: Neural-type processes from MIH-secreting cells intermingle with the muscle fibres of surrounding epitheliomuscular cells.
source: A variable number of neural-type processes containing prominent microtubule bundles project basally from these cells (Figure 5E,F), and intermingle with the muscle fibres of surrounding epitheliomuscular cells (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: The cell nuclei of MIH-secreting cells are generally located more basally than those of the surrounding epitheliomuscular cells.
source: The cell nuclei were generally located more basally than those of the surrounding epitheliomuscular cells (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A, C.

claim: Most of the peptide hormone (MIH) is secreted at distance from its site of action at the oocyte surface.
source: This configuration implies that most of the peptide hormone (MIH) is secreted at distance from its site of action at the oocyte surface, consistent with a neuroendocrine function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial configuration observed in immunofluorescence images.

claim: The spatial configuration of MIH secretion is consistent with a neuroendocrine function.
source: This configuration implies that most of the peptide hormone (MIH) is secreted at distance from its site of action at the oocyte surface, consistent with a neuroendocrine function.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the observed spatial organization.

claim: MIH-positive cells do not have extensive apical domains exposed on the external face of the ectodermal epithelium.
source: MIH-positive cells did not have extensive apical domains exposed on the external face of the ectodermal epithelium, although MIH staining was in some cases detected very close to this surface at the interstices between surrounding myoepithelial cells (Figure 5C' and D").
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence observations shown in Figures 5C' and D".

claim: MIH staining was in some cases detected very close to the gonad surface at the interstices between surrounding myoepithelial cells.
source: MIH-positive cells did not have extensive apical domains exposed on the external face of the ectodermal epithelium, although MIH staining was in some cases detected very close to this surface at the interstices between surrounding myoepithelial cells (Figure 5C' and D").
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence observations shown in Figures 5C' and D".

claim: Cilia could not be unambiguously associated with the MIH-secreting cells.
source: Cilia, which decorated most epitheliomuscular cells, could not be unambiguously associated with the MIH-secreting cells (Figure 5F,G), but basal bodies could be detected in the apical side of these cells with a gamma-tubulin antibody (Figure 5H–H').
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figures 5F-G.

claim: Basal bodies could be detected in the apical side of MIH-secreting cells with a gamma-tubulin antibody.
source: Cilia, which decorated most epitheliomuscular cells, could not be unambiguously associated with the MIH-secreting cells (Figure 5F,G), but basal bodies could be detected in the apical side of these cells with a gamma-tubulin antibody (Figure 5H–H').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5H-H'.

claim: The MIH-secreting cells have morphological features characteristic of multipolar neurosensory cells in cnidarians.
source: These various immunofluorescence analyses indicate that the MIH-secreting cells have morphological features characteristic of multipolar neurosensory cells in cnidarians (Saripalli and Westfall, 1996).
evidence: The claim is inferred from immunofluorescence observations and supported by citation.

claim: All 10 Clytia Opsins fell within the cnidops group in phylogenetic analysis.
source: All 10 Clytia Opsins fell as expected within the cnidops group, with Opsin9 and the closely-related Opsin10 having more divergent sequences than the other Clytia opsins (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Opsin9 and Opsin10 have more divergent sequences than the other Clytia opsins.
source: All 10 Clytia Opsins fell as expected within the cnidops group, with Opsin9 and the closely-related Opsin10 having more divergent sequences than the other Clytia opsins (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clytia Opsin9 and Opsin10 genes contain a distinct intron, unlike all other described medusozoan Cnidops genes.
source: The draft Clytia genome sequence (Leclère et al., 2016) further revealed that Clytia Opsin9 and Opsin10 genes contain a distinct intron, unlike all other described medusozoan Cnidops genes, in a distinct position to those found in available Anthozoan Opsin II, Anthozoan Cnidops and Xenopsin genes (Vöcking et al., 2017; Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome sequence analysis and cited references.

claim: The intron in Clytia Opsin9 and Opsin10 is in a distinct position to those found in available Anthozoan Opsin II, Anthozoan Cnidops and Xenopsin genes.
source: The draft Clytia genome sequence (Leclère et al., 2016) further revealed that Clytia Opsin9 and Opsin10 genes contain a distinct intron, unlike all other described medusozoan Cnidops genes, in a distinct position to those found in available Anthozoan Opsin II, Anthozoan Cnidops and Xenopsin genes (Vöcking et al., 2017; Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome sequence analysis and cited references.

claim: The Clytia Opsin9 amino acid sequence exhibits all the hallmarks of a functional photopigment.
source: Despite this picture of rapid evolutionary divergence of Clytia Opsin9/Opsin10 within the diversifying cnidops family, the Clytia Opsin9 amino acid sequence exhibits all the hallmarks of a functional photopigment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clytia Opsin9 has conserved amino acids at positions required for critical disulphide bond formation and for Schiff base linkage to the retinal chromophore.
source: It has conserved amino acids at positions required for critical disulphide bond formation and for Schiff base linkage to the retinal chromophore (Fischer et al., 2013; Gehring, 2014; Schnitzler et al., 2012), including acidic residues at the both potential 'counterion' positions, only one of which is largely conserved in cnidarian opsin sequences (Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and cited references.

claim: Clytia Opsin9 has acidic residues at both potential 'counterion' positions, only one of which is largely conserved in cnidarian opsin sequences.
source: It has conserved amino acids at positions required for critical disulphide bond formation and for Schiff base linkage to the retinal chromophore (Fischer et al., 2013; Gehring, 2014; Schnitzler et al., 2012), including acidic residues at the both potential 'counterion' positions, only one of which is largely conserved in cnidarian opsin sequences (Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and cited reference.

claim: The Glu/Asp-Arg-Tyr/Phe motif adjacent to the third transmembrane domain, involved in cytoplasmic signal transduction via G proteins, is present in Opsin9.
source: The Glu/Asp-Arg-Tyr/Phe motif adjacent to the third transmembrane domain, involved in cytoplasmic signal transduction via G proteins (Fischer et al., 2013; Kojima et al., 2000; Schnitzler et al., 2012) is also present in Opsin9.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and cited references.

claim: Clytia Opsin9 is not orthologous to the opsin genes previously identified as expressed in the gonad of the hydromedusa Cladonema.
source: We could show unambiguously, however, from our phylogenetic reconstructions (Figure 6B) and AU ('approximately unbiased') phylogenetic tests (Shimodaira, 2002), that Clytia Opsin9 is not orthologous to the opsin genes previously identified as expressed in the gonad of the hydromedusa Cladonema (AU test: p<1e−7) or the cubomedusa Tripedalia (AU test: p<1e−20).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and AU tests.

claim: Clytia Opsin9 is not orthologous to the opsin genes previously identified as expressed in the gonad of the cubomedusa Tripedalia.
source: We could show unambiguously, however, from our phylogenetic reconstructions (Figure 6B) and AU ('approximately unbiased') phylogenetic tests (Shimodaira, 2002), that Clytia Opsin9 is not orthologous to the opsin genes previously identified as expressed in the gonad of the hydromedusa Cladonema (AU test: p<1e−7) or the cubomedusa Tripedalia (AU test: p<1e−20).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and AU tests.

claim: Diversification of the cnidops gene family in Medusozoa was accompanied by expression of different opsin paralogs in the gonad in different species.
source: Thus diversification of the cnidops gene family in Medusozoa was accompanied by expression of different opsin paralogs in the gonad in different species.
evidence: The claim is inferred from phylogenetic analysis showing non-orthologous gonad-expressed opsins.

claim: Clytia Opsin9 is required for a direct light-response mechanism that acts locally in the gonad to trigger gamete maturation and release.
source: To summarise the results of this study, we have provided the first demonstration, using CRISPR/Cas9–mediated gene knockout, of an essential role for an opsin gene in non-visual photodetection in a cnidarian. Clytia Opsin9 is required for a direct light-response mechanism that acts locally in the gonad to trigger gamete maturation and release (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion from all experimental results.

claim: Opsin9 occurs in specialised sensory-secretory cells of the Clytia gonad ectoderm to trigger MIH secretion from these cells upon light reception.
source: It occurs in specialised sensory-secretory cells of the Clytia gonad ectoderm to trigger MIH secretion from these cells upon light reception.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion from expression, localization, and functional studies.

claim: MIH induces oocyte maturation in females and release of motile sperm in males.
source: This peptidic MIH in turn induces oocyte maturation in females, and also release of motile sperm in males (Takeda et al., 2018), efficiently synchronising spawning to maximise reproductive success.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takeda et al., 2018.

claim: MIH efficiently synchronises spawning to maximise reproductive success.
source: This peptidic MIH in turn induces oocyte maturation in females, and also release of motile sperm in males (Takeda et al., 2018), efficiently synchronising spawning to maximise reproductive success.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the biological function of MIH-mediated spawning synchronization.

claim: The MIH-secreting cells of the gonad ectoderm in Clytia show parallels with deep brain photoreceptor cells in vertebrates.
source: Our study on opsins has further revealed a parallel between the MIH-secreting cells of the gonad ectoderm in Clytia and deep brain photoreceptor cells in vertebrates, as well as equivalent cells in various protostome species that regulate physiological responses through neurohormone release in response to ambient light (Fernandes et al., 2013; Fischer et al., 2013; Halford et al., 2009; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited literature on vertebrate and protostome photoreceptor cells.

claim: TSH-producing cells in birds and fish pituitary show opsin-related photodetection, secrete neuropeptide hormones and are implicated in hormonal control of reproduction.
source: Like the Clytia MIH-producing cells, TSH-producing cells in birds and fish pituitary (Nakane et al., 2013; Vigh et al., 2002), and vasopressin/oxytocin-expressing cells in fish hypothalamus and annelid forebrain (Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007), show opsin-related photodetection, secrete neuropeptide hormones and are implicated in hormonal control of reproduction (Juntti and Fernald, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Vasopressin/oxytocin-expressing cells in fish hypothalamus and annelid forebrain show opsin-related photodetection, secrete neuropeptide hormones and are implicated in hormonal control of reproduction.
source: Like the Clytia MIH-producing cells, TSH-producing cells in birds and fish pituitary (Nakane et al., 2013; Vigh et al., 2002), and vasopressin/oxytocin-expressing cells in fish hypothalamus and annelid forebrain (Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007), show opsin-related photodetection, secrete neuropeptide hormones and are implicated in hormonal control of reproduction (Juntti and Fernald, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The putative neurosecretory cell type associated with the germ line that regulated gamete release in ancestral metazoans was also photosensitive.
source: We can thus propose that the putative neurosecretory cell type associated with the germ line that regulated gamete release in ancestral metazoans was also photosensitive.
evidence: The claim is a speculative evolutionary proposal based on comparative analysis.

claim: The active photopigments in ancestral metazoan neurosecretory cells could have been cryptochromes or animal opsins.
source: The active photopigments in these cells could have been cryptochromes, the most ancient metazoan photopigment family inherited from unicellular ancestors (Cronin and Porter, 2014; Gehring, 2014) or animal opsins, whose gene family is absent in sponges but expanded extensively in both cnidarians and bilaterians from a common ancestral GPCR gene (Feuda et al., 2014; 2012; Gehring, 2014; Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations about photopigment evolution.

claim: Cryptochromes are the most ancient metazoan photopigment family inherited from unicellular ancestors.
source: The active photopigments in these cells could have been cryptochromes, the most ancient metazoan photopigment family inherited from unicellular ancestors (Cronin and Porter, 2014; Gehring, 2014) or animal opsins, whose gene family is absent in sponges but expanded extensively in both cnidarians and bilaterians from a common ancestral GPCR gene (Feuda et al., 2014; 2012; Gehring, 2014; Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The animal opsin gene family is absent in sponges but expanded extensively in both cnidarians and bilaterians from a common ancestral GPCR gene.
source: The active photopigments in these cells could have been cryptochromes, the most ancient metazoan photopigment family inherited from unicellular ancestors (Cronin and Porter, 2014; Gehring, 2014) or animal opsins, whose gene family is absent in sponges but expanded extensively in both cnidarians and bilaterians from a common ancestral GPCR gene (Feuda et al., 2014; 2012; Gehring, 2014; Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Opsin9 protein in Clytia replaced the ancestral photopigment in the MIH-secreting cells during cnidarian evolution to provide optimised spawning responses to particular light wavelength and intensity.
source: Under this evolutionary scenario, the essential Opsin9 protein in Clytia, and similarly the gonad-expressed Cladonema (Suga et al., 2008) and Tripedalia (Liegertová et al., 2015) opsins, would have replaced the ancestral photopigment in the MIH-secreting cells during cnidarian evolution to provide optimised spawning responses to particular light wavelength and intensity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative evolutionary scenario based on the findings.

claim: Deployment of animal opsins is thought to have allowed more rapid and precise photoresponses than the ancestral cryptochrome system in the evolution of vision in eumetazoans.
source: A parallel can be drawn with the evolution of vision in eumetazoans, in which deployment of animal opsins is thought to have allowed more rapid and precise photoresponses than the ancestral cryptochrome system (Gehring, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cnidarians are characterised by the lack of a centralised nervous system.
source: Cnidarians are characterised by the lack of a centralised nervous system, and correspondingly show localised regulation of many physiological processes and behaviours at the organ, tissue or even the cellular levels.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cnidarian biology.

claim: Cnidarians show localised regulation of many physiological processes and behaviours at the organ, tissue or even the cellular levels.
source: Cnidarians are characterised by the lack of a centralised nervous system, and correspondingly show localised regulation of many physiological processes and behaviours at the organ, tissue or even the cellular levels.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cnidarian biology.

claim: Clytia Opsin9 is the first cnidarian opsin to have a demonstrated function.
source: Clytia Opsin9, the first cnidarian opsin to have a demonstrated function, is expressed in the scattered, MIH-secreting cells, which act autonomously in the gonad without any need for input from other parts of the medusa.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from the functional demonstration via CRISPR/Cas9 knockout.

claim: MIH-secreting cells act autonomously in the gonad without any need for input from other parts of the medusa.
source: Clytia Opsin9, the first cnidarian opsin to have a demonstrated function, is expressed in the scattered, MIH-secreting cells, which act autonomously in the gonad without any need for input from other parts of the medusa.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing isolated gonads respond to light.

claim: Expansion of the opsin gene family within the hydrozoan clade was accompanied by the local deployment of individual opsins with specific spectral characteristics adjusted to regulate a variety of physiological behaviours in response to light.
source: Our findings support a scenario in which expansion of the opsin gene family within the hydrozoan clade was accompanied by the local deployment of individual opsins with specific spectral characteristics adjusted to regulate a variety of physiological behaviours in response to light, epitomised by Clytia Opsin9 and its regulation of spawning.
evidence: The claim is a speculative evolutionary scenario supported by the findings.

claim: In hydrozoan jellyfish, spawning is triggered by dark-light or light-dark transitions acting on the gonad.
source: In hydrozoan jellyfish, spawning is triggered by dark-light or light-dark transitions acting on the gonad, and is mediated by oocyte maturation-inducing neuropeptide hormones (MIHs) released from the ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by cited literature.

claim: Spawning in hydrozoan jellyfish is mediated by oocyte maturation-inducing neuropeptide hormones (MIHs) released from the ectoderm.
source: In hydrozoan jellyfish, spawning is triggered by dark-light or light-dark transitions acting on the gonad, and is mediated by oocyte maturation-inducing neuropeptide hormones (MIHs) released from the ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by cited literature.

claim: Opsin9 knockout jellyfish generated by CRISPR/Cas9 failed to undergo oocyte maturation and spawning.
source: Opsin9 knockout jellyfish generated by CRISPR/Cas9 failed to undergo oocyte maturation and spawning, a phenotype reversible by synthetic MIH.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results.

claim: The spawning failure phenotype in Opsin9 knockout jellyfish is reversible by synthetic MIH.
source: Opsin9 knockout jellyfish generated by CRISPR/Cas9 failed to undergo oocyte maturation and spawning, a phenotype reversible by synthetic MIH.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results.

claim: Gamete maturation and release in Clytia is regulated by gonadal photosensory-neurosecretory cells that secrete MIH in response to light via Opsin9.
source: Gamete maturation and release in Clytia is thus regulated by gonadal photosensory-neurosecretory cells that secrete MIH in response to light via Opsin9.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by all experimental results.

claim: Similar cells in ancestral eumetazoans may have allowed tissue-level photo-regulation of diverse behaviours.
source: Similar cells in ancestral eumetazoans may have allowed tissue-level photo-regulation of diverse behaviours, a feature elaborated in cnidarians in parallel with expansion of the opsin gene family.
evidence: The claim is a speculative evolutionary proposal stated in the abstract.

claim: Tissue-level photo-regulation of diverse behaviours is a feature elaborated in cnidarians in parallel with expansion of the opsin gene family.
source: Similar cells in ancestral eumetazoans may have allowed tissue-level photo-regulation of diverse behaviours, a feature elaborated in cnidarians in parallel with expansion of the opsin gene family.
evidence: The claim is a speculative evolutionary proposal stated in the abstract.

claim: Integration of environmental light information contributes to tight coordination of gamete release in a wide range of animal species.
source: Integration of environmental light information contributes to tight coordination of gamete release in a wide range of animal species.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents general knowledge in the field.

claim: The nature of the photodetection systems involved in gamete release and their evolutionary origins are poorly understood.
source: The nature of the photodetection systems involved and their evolutionary origins are poorly undestood.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: Light cues can provide immediate triggers for gamete release, which integrate with seasonal and/or circadian regulation.
source: Light cues can also provide more immediate triggers for gamete release, which integrate with seasonal and/or circadian regulation (Kaniewska et al., 2015; Lambert and Brandt, 1967), but the involvement of specific photopigments in such regulation has not previously been addressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The involvement of specific photopigments in immediate light-triggered gamete release has not previously been addressed.
source: Light cues can also provide more immediate triggers for gamete release, which integrate with seasonal and/or circadian regulation (Kaniewska et al., 2015; Lambert and Brandt, 1967), but the involvement of specific photopigments in such regulation has not previously been addressed.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: Members of Hydrozoa commonly display light-regulated sexual reproduction.
source: Members of Hydrozoa, a subgroup of Cnidaria which can have medusae or polyps as the sexual form, commonly display light-regulated sexual reproduction (Leclère et al., 2016; Siebert and Juliano, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hydrozoans have simple gonads in which the germ cells are sandwiched between ectoderm and endoderm.
source: They have simple gonads in which the germ cells are sandwiched between ectoderm and endoderm, and unlike many other animals they lack additional layers of somatic follicle cells surrounding oocytes in the female (Deguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Hydrozoans lack additional layers of somatic follicle cells surrounding oocytes in the female.
source: They have simple gonads in which the germ cells are sandwiched between ectoderm and endoderm, and unlike many other animals they lack additional layers of somatic follicle cells surrounding oocytes in the female (Deguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Light-dark and/or dark-light transitions trigger the release of mature gametes into the seawater by rupture of the gonad ectoderm in hydrozoans.
source: Light-dark and/or dark-light transitions trigger the release of mature gametes into the seawater by rupture of the gonad ectoderm (Freeman and Ridgway, 1988; Miller, 1979; Roosen-Runge, 1962).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gamete release is coordinated with diel migration behaviours in jellyfish to ensure gamete proximity for fertilisation.
source: Gamete release is coordinated with diel migration behaviours in jellyfish to ensure gamete proximity for fertilisation (Martin, 2002; Mills, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The photodetection systems that mediate hydrozoan spawning operate locally within the gonads.
source: We know that the photodetection systems that mediate hydrozoan spawning operate locally within the gonads, since isolated gonads will spawn upon dark-light or light-dark transitions (Freeman, 1987; Ikegami et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature showing isolated gonads respond to light.

claim: Isolated hydrozoan gonads will spawn upon dark-light or light-dark transitions.
source: We know that the photodetection systems that mediate hydrozoan spawning operate locally within the gonads, since isolated gonads will spawn upon dark-light or light-dark transitions (Freeman, 1987; Ikegami et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Expression of certain opsin genes has been reported in the gonads of the hydrozoan jellyfish Cladonema radiatum.
source: Opsin gene families have been identified in cnidarians and provide good candidates for a role in this process, with expression of certain opsin genes reported in the gonads both of the hydrozoan jellyfish Cladonema radiatum (Suga et al., 2008) and of the cubozoan jellyfish Tripedalia cystophora (Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Expression of certain opsin genes has been reported in the gonads of the cubozoan jellyfish Tripedalia cystophora.
source: Opsin gene families have been identified in cnidarians and provide good candidates for a role in this process, with expression of certain opsin genes reported in the gonads both of the hydrozoan jellyfish Cladonema radiatum (Suga et al., 2008) and of the cubozoan jellyfish Tripedalia cystophora (Liegertová et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In female hydrozoans, the regulation of spawning is tightly coupled to oocyte maturation.
source: In female hydrozoans, the regulation of spawning is tightly coupled to oocyte maturation, the process by which resting ovarian oocytes resume meiosis to be transformed into fertilisable eggs (Yamashita et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Oocyte maturation is the process by which resting ovarian oocytes resume meiosis to be transformed into fertilisable eggs.
source: In female hydrozoans, the regulation of spawning is tightly coupled to oocyte maturation, the process by which resting ovarian oocytes resume meiosis to be transformed into fertilisable eggs (Yamashita et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents established biological knowledge.

claim: Oocyte maturation, followed by spawning, is induced by 'Maturation Inducing Hormones' (MIHs) released from gonad somatic tissues upon reception of the appropriate light cue.
source: Oocyte maturation, followed by spawning, is induced by 'Maturation Inducing Hormones' (MIHs), released from gonad somatic tissues upon reception of the appropriate light cue (Freeman, 1987; Ikegami et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The molecular identity of MIH of several hydrozoan species has been uncovered as PRPamide family tetrapeptides.
source: The molecular identity of MIH of several hydrozoan species has been uncovered recently as PRPamide family tetrapeptides, which are released from scattered cells with neural-type morphology present in the gonad ectoderm following dark-light transitions (Takeda et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takeda et al., 2018.

claim: MIH peptides are released from scattered cells with neural-type morphology present in the gonad ectoderm following dark-light transitions.
source: The molecular identity of MIH of several hydrozoan species has been uncovered recently as PRPamide family tetrapeptides, which are released from scattered cells with neural-type morphology present in the gonad ectoderm following dark-light transitions (Takeda et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takeda et al., 2018.

claim: MIH release in Clytia gonads is triggered by a light cue after a minimum dark period of 1–2 hr.
source: MIH release in Clytia gonads is triggered by a light cue after a minimum dark period of 1–2 hr, with mature eggs being released two hours later (Amiel et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mature eggs are released two hours after MIH release in Clytia.
source: MIH release in Clytia gonads is triggered by a light cue after a minimum dark period of 1–2 hr, with mature eggs being released two hours later (Amiel et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Oocyte maturation is accompanied by breakdown of the membrane of the oocyte nucleus ('GV' for germinal vesicle) in fully-grown oocytes, followed by polar body emmission and spawning.
source: Oocyte maturation is accompanied by breakdown of the membrane of the oocyte nucleus ('GV' for germinal vesicle) in fully-grown oocytes, followed by polar body emmission and spawning.
evidence: The claim describes the biological process of oocyte maturation observed in the study.

claim: A total of 20–30 gonads were analysed per wavelength in the monochromator assay.
source: A total of 20–30 gonads were analysed per wavelength.
evidence: The claim describes the sample size in the experimental design shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The high expression of Opsin9 gene in the gonad ectoderm made it a strong candidate for involvement in light-induced spawning.
source: The high expression of Opsin9 gene in the gonad ectoderm made it a strong candidate for involvement in light-induced spawning.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the expression data that guided the functional studies.

claim: Over 86% of cells expressing either Opsin9 or PP4 co-expressed both genes in 10 different gonads.
source: Of n = 594 randomly chosen cells expressing either gene counted in 10 different gonads, over 86% co-expressed Opsin9 and PP4 mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of double fluorescent in situ hybridization data.

claim: This finding raised the possibility that spawning in Clytia might be directly controlled by light detection through an opsin photopigment in the MIH-secreting cells of the gonad ectoderm.
source: This finding raised the possibility that spawning in Clytia might be directly controlled by light detection through an opsin photopigment in the MIH-secreting cells of the gonad ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the co-expression data that motivated the knockout experiments.

claim: CRISPR guide RNAs were designed to target a site in the first exon of Opsin9 encoding the third transmembrane domain.
source: CRISPR guide RNAs were designed to target a site in the first exon of Opsin9 encoding the third transmembrane domain, and were verified not to match any other sites in available Clytia genome sequences.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design of the CRISPR/Cas9 approach.

claim: The CRISPR guide RNAs were verified not to match any other sites in available Clytia genome sequences.
source: CRISPR guide RNAs were designed to target a site in the first exon of Opsin9 encoding the third transmembrane domain, and were verified not to match any other sites in available Clytia genome sequences.
evidence: The claim describes the specificity verification of the CRISPR/Cas9 approach.

claim: The 5 bp deletion in Opsin9n1_4 leads to a frame-shift and an early STOP codon.
source: This mutation leads to a frame-shift and an early STOP codon in Opsin9n1_4 (orange box).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The dominant 5 bp deletion and a long 21 bp deletion were detected in 10/11 Opsin9n1_4 medusae with the spawning-impaired phenotype.
source: The dominant 5 bp deletion and a long 21 bp deletion were detected in 10/11 medusae.
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Opsin9n1_4 medusae without phenotype showed an increased proportion of sequences with no mutation, higher mosaicism and a lower ratio of frame-shift mutations.
source: 3D-graph showing the mutation rate and type of 8 independent Opsin9n1_4 jellyfish with no phenotype. These medusae showed an increased proportion of sequences with no mutation, higher mosaicism and a lower ratio of frame-shift mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fisher's exact test showed a significant difference (at p<0.01) between spawning in wild type and mutant samples stimulated by light.
source: Fisher's exact test showed a significant difference (at p<0.01) between spawning in wild type and mutant samples stimulated by light (D), but not by MIH (E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Fisher's exact test showed no significant difference between spawning in wild type and mutant samples stimulated by MIH.
source: Fisher's exact test showed a significant difference (at p<0.01) between spawning in wild type and mutant samples stimulated by light (D), but not by MIH (E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Mann-Whitney U test showed a significant difference between MIH fluorescence in wild type gonads with and without light stimulation (at p<0.01).
source: The Mann-Whitney U test showed a significant difference between conditions (at p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mann-Whitney U test did not show a significant difference in MIH fluorescence in Opsin9n1_4 gonads with and without light stimulation at p<0.01.
source: Mann-Whitney U test did not show a significant difference at p<0.01.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Basal myofibres of epitheliomuscular cells form a layer over the oocytes and stain strongly with phalloidin fluorescent probes.
source: These basal myofibres form a layer over the oocytes and stain strongly with phalloidin fluorescent probes (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A-D.

claim: In regions overlying large oocytes, the gonad ectoderm is elevated by a characteristic space on the basal side.
source: In regions overlying large oocytes, the gonad ectoderm, including most of the MIH-rich basal processes, was elevated by a characteristic space on the basal side (Figure 5C), probably reflecting the accumulation of extracellular jelly components around oocytes during late stages of growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The space elevating the gonad ectoderm over large oocytes probably reflects the accumulation of extracellular jelly components around oocytes during late stages of growth.
source: In regions overlying large oocytes, the gonad ectoderm, including most of the MIH-rich basal processes, was elevated by a characteristic space on the basal side (Figure 5C), probably reflecting the accumulation of extracellular jelly components around oocytes during late stages of growth.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the cause of the observed space.

claim: The traditional division of opsins into 'c-opsins' and 'r-opsins' is no longer adequate as a representation of opsin phylogenetic relationships.
source: With increasing availability of opsin gene sequences covering a widening range of animal taxa, the traditional division into 'c-opsins', expressed in ciliary photoreceptor cells such as vertebrate rods and cones, and 'r-opsins,' as expressed in arthropod rhabdomeric photoreceptors, is clearly no longer adequate as a representation of opsin phylogenetic relationships (Cronin and Porter, 2014; Feuda et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Molecular phylogeny analyses are progressively revealing a complicated evolutionary history for the opsins, involving many gene duplications and losses in separate animal lineages.
source: Molecular phylogeny analyses are progressively revealing a complicated evolutionary history for the opsins, involving many gene duplications and losses in separate animal lineages, starting from a set of at least nine genes in the common ancestor of Bilateria, with three or four sequences already present before the cnidarian-bilaterian split (Ramirez et al., 2016; Vöcking et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At least nine opsin genes were present in the common ancestor of Bilateria.
source: Molecular phylogeny analyses are progressively revealing a complicated evolutionary history for the opsins, involving many gene duplications and losses in separate animal lineages, starting from a set of at least nine genes in the common ancestor of Bilateria, with three or four sequences already present before the cnidarian-bilaterian split (Ramirez et al., 2016; Vöcking et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Three or four opsin sequences were already present before the cnidarian-bilaterian split.
source: Molecular phylogeny analyses are progressively revealing a complicated evolutionary history for the opsins, involving many gene duplications and losses in separate animal lineages, starting from a set of at least nine genes in the common ancestor of Bilateria, with three or four sequences already present before the cnidarian-bilaterian split (Ramirez et al., 2016; Vöcking et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Available cnidarian opsin sequences form three groups, termed 'anthozoan opsin I', 'anthozoan opsin II' and 'cnidops'.
source: Available cnidarian opsin sequences form three groups, termed 'anthozoan opsin I', 'anthozoan opsin II' and 'cnidops'.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis of cnidarian opsins.

claim: The anthozoan opsin I and anthozoan opsin II groups contain only anthozoan (coral and sea anemone) sequences.
source: The first two contain only anthozoan (coral and sea anemone) sequences.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis of cnidarian opsins.

claim: The cnidops group includes some anthozoan opsins and all published opsin genes from the medusozoan clade (jellyfish and hydra).
source: The cnidops group includes some anthozoan opsins and all published opsin genes from the medusozoan clade (jellyfish and hydra), and is probably the sister group to the xenopsin group, which includes opsins from a few disparate protostome taxa (Ramirez et al., 2016; Vöcking et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis and cited references.

claim: The cnidops group is probably the sister group to the xenopsin group.
source: The cnidops group includes some anthozoan opsins and all published opsin genes from the medusozoan clade (jellyfish and hydra), and is probably the sister group to the xenopsin group, which includes opsins from a few disparate protostome taxa (Ramirez et al., 2016; Vöcking et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis and cited references.

claim: The xenopsin group includes opsins from a few disparate protostome taxa.
source: The cnidops group includes some anthozoan opsins and all published opsin genes from the medusozoan clade (jellyfish and hydra), and is probably the sister group to the xenopsin group, which includes opsins from a few disparate protostome taxa (Ramirez et al., 2016; Vöcking et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The exact relationship of Clytia Opsin9/10 to other medusozoan opsins cannot be resolved with the available data.
source: The exact relationship of Clytia Opsin9/10 to other medusozoan opsins cannot be resolved with the available data.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from phylogenetic analyses showing unstable tree topologies.

claim: The phylogenetic position of Clytia Opsin9/10 was found to be unstable when analysed using different evolutionary models and datasets.
source: Their phylogenetic position was found to be unstable when analysed using different evolutionary models and datasets (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claim: Extensive sampling from more medusozoan species will be needed to fully resolve the phylogenetic history of Clytia Opsin9/10.
source: Extensive sampling from more medusozoan species will be needed to fully resolve their phylogenetic history.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion about the limitations of current phylogenetic analysis.

claim: At dawn, light activates Opsin9 in specialised cells of the gonad epithelium, causing secretion of MIH inside the gonad.
source: At dawn, light activates Opsin9 in specialised cells of the gonad epithelium, causing secretion of MIH inside the gonad.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: MIH acts on the oocyte surface to trigger the resumption of meiosis, followed by Germinal Vesicle breakdown (GVBD) and oocyte maturation.
source: MIH in turn acts on the oocyte surface to trigger the resumption of meiosis, followed by Germinal Vesicle breakdown (GVBD) and oocyte maturation.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings illustrated in Figure 7 and supported by cited literature.
